cognate: Ved. mātā́ / mātár ~ Gk μήτηρ (exact, *méh₂tēr) as title of the Earth; on the father side Ved. dyaúḥ pitā́ / voc. dyaùḥ pítar ~ Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ (support, Il. 1.503 etc.) ~ Lat. Iuppiter (recalled), *dyéw ph₂ter.
drift_or_renewal: Greek renews the Sky partner of Earth with Οὐρανός (the inherited *dyéws became the personal god Zeus, who keeps the 'father' title separately); the Earth word is renewed in both (Ved. pṛthivī / bhūmi, Gk Γαῖα / γῆ; Ved. pṛthivī́ itself is cognate with Πλάταια, recalled). AVŚ 12.1.12 shows the father slot is substitutable inside Vedic too (parjanyaḥ pitā, the rain god), which matches Lucretius' raining Pater aether.
shared_syntax: Nominal sentences / vocatives pairing 'Sky (is) father' with 'Earth (is) mother', the Earth bearing the title 'mother' as an appositive or predicate (Ved. pṛthivī́ mātā́; Gk θεῶν μήτηρ, Γαῖα μάτηρ, γῆ πάντων μήτηρ); in the Greek hymn the mother is addressed as consort of Sky (ἄλοχ’ Οὐρανοῦ), the Vedic pair is a dual merism (dyā́vā-pṛthivī́).
context: Both are hymnic invocations of Earth as cosmic mother conferring prosperity: AVŚ 12.1 is the Vedic Hymn to Earth (12.1.12 'Earth is mother, I am son of Earth; Parjanya is father, may he help us'), and HH 30 is the Greek Hymn to Earth Mother of All (vv. 16-17: those she honours prosper; 'hail, mother of gods, wife of starry Ouranos'). The Vedic pair recurs as a protective formula in AV charms (AVP 1.12.5, AVŚ 2.28.7). The congruence is a specific divine couple with fixed kinship titles, not mere co-occurrence of 'mother'. Caveat: the Greek cognate words sit in the context line (17) of the anchor passage, not in line 16 itself; Ved. dyaús/Gk Zeus = Lat. Iuppiter identification is recalled from the literature.

note: No defensible inherited phrase. The packet's shared element is the root *bʰendʰ- 'bind', but as different lexemes with no shared second term or setting (Ved. bandh-/bándhu- 'bind, kinsman'; Gk πεῖσμα 'ship's cable', φάτνη 'manger'; Lat. funis 'rope' in Cato's inventories, a doubtful mapping; OE bend): shared vocabulary, not phraseology. The Vedic vr̥trám/áhim ... ávadhīt lines are the well-known 'slew the serpent' formula, here with no second-branch anchor (and the verb is the suppletive vadh-). Mapping errors that seeded the Vedic block: asita- 'black (snake)' is mapped to *sinéh₂ti 'bind' and vadh- 'slay' (*wedʰh₁-) to *wedʰ- 'lead, marry'. Latvian dainas with vest 'lead (a bride)' (BV 15975, 18190) have no cognate partner in the packet; Gk ζεύγνυμι γάμοις (Eur. Hel. 1654, Alc. 994) is a different metaphor (*yewg-).

cognate: Lat. daps 'sacrificial feast' and Gk δαπάνη / δάπτω share *dh₂p- (recalled: Benveniste's 'dépense' set, with ON tafn 'sacrificial animal', Arm. tawn 'feast'); the lexicon's mapping of Gk δεῖπνον to the same root is the weak link (its etymology is disputed in the handbooks, recalled).
drift_or_renewal: Latin keeps the sacral sense (daps offered to Jupiter Dapalis, pollucere, macte); Greek δεῖπνον is overwhelmingly secular 'meal' (in-packet Od. 17.214, Il. 2.399, Op. 442, Thgn. 999, Pers. 375), and the root otherwise drifted to 'expense' (δαπάνη, Bacch. 893) and 'devour' (δάπτω, Il. 23.183, PV 370). Sacral δεῖπνα to gods in tragedy could be a residue or a secondary use.
shared_syntax: Noun 'ritual feast' as object of a verb of making/giving with a divine dative recipient: Lat. dapem facere / dare + dat. (Ioui, Minotauro); Gk δεῖπνα (θυσίας τε) ... θεοῖς ὁπλίζεσθαι, δεῖπνα ... ἔθυον.
context: All anchors are ritual meals for supernatural recipients: Cato's prescribed daps to Jupiter Dapalis before ploughing; Catullus' tribute 'feast' of youths for the Minotaur; Xuthus' feasts and sacrifices to the gods (Ion); the Erinyes' nocturnal feasts burned on the fire-hearth (Eum.). The secure Greek member δαπάνα (Bacch. 893) is itself in a religious statement (it 'costs little' to hold that the divine has power), and the δεῖπνον passages carry the ritual-meal congruence. Weakness: only the Latin side is clearly the inherited sacral term; on the Greek side the specific word and its etymology are uncertain, so this may be a lexical-semantic match rather than a phrase.

cognate: Fire word Gk πῦρ ~ OE fȳr (*péh₂wr̥) in the anchors; the 'eat' verb is *h₁ed- in Gk ἐσθίει (Il. 23.182), OE fretan < *fra-etan (Beo. 3015, 3115) and Ved. kravy-ā́d-, atti of Agni (RV 10.16.9, 1.143.5) — all in support loci, not in the anchor lines.
drift_or_renewal: Greek also uses δάπτω 'devour' (Il. 23.183, PV 370) and OE forswelgan 'swallow' (Beo. 1123); Vedic renews the fire word with agní-. Ved. jámbha- 'jaws' (RV 1.143.5) vs Gk γνάθοι (PV 370) are not cognate.
shared_syntax: Fire as agent subject of a verb of eating with the dead (or their goods) as object: πάντας πῦρ ἐσθίει; Nū sceal glēd fretan (wigena strengel); kravyā́d- agní 'flesh-eating fire'.
context: Cremation: the pyre of Patroclus with the twelve Trojans (Il. 23.182-3), the pyre of Beowulf (Beo. 3115, 3144) with the treasure 'which the fire shall devour' (3015), and the Vedic cremation fire kravyā́d (RV 10.16). Weakness: 'devouring fire' is typologically common (e.g. Hebrew), and *h₁ed- is the basic verb 'eat' in all three, so chance is a real possibility; the anchor lines themselves carry the fire word and the pyre setting, the shared verb only in support.

cognate: Derivative of *h₂eydʰ- 'kindle, blaze' as epithet of fire: Ved. samidhāná-/sámiddha- (√idh-) + agní-; Lat. aesti-fer (aestus < *h₂eydʰ-tu-) + ignis, where ignis = Ved. agní- exactly; Gk αἰθόμενος + πῦρ.
drift_or_renewal: Greek renews the animate fire noun *h₁n̥gʷnis with inanimate πῦρ; Latin keeps *h₁n̥gʷnis (ignis) like Vedic but expresses the *h₂eydʰ- element through the noun aestus in a -fer compound (possibly Lucretius' own coinage) instead of a participle. Vedic idh- is specialised for ritual kindling, Greek αἴθομαι and Lat. aestus are descriptive.
shared_syntax: Noun 'fire' + agreeing epithet built on *h₂eydʰ- (Ved. middle participle, Gk middle participle in the line-end formula πυρὸς (μένος) αἰθομένοιο, Lat. compound adjective).
context: Fire described by its blaze: Vedic ritual Agni 'kindled' (RV 7.44.1b agním sámiddham, 8.25.19c, 5.28.5a), Greek descriptive similes (Chimaera's breath Th. 324 = Il. 6.182, the lamp-glow Od. 19.39), Lucretius' physics of fire emitting light and heat (1.663). What argues against pure chance is the Latin-Vedic pairing of the same animate noun *h₁n̥gʷnis with a *h₂eydʰ- derivative, matched in Greek with the renewed noun; what argues for chance is that *h₂eydʰ- is the basic verb of burning, the contexts are not ritually parallel, and aestifer may be a learned coinage. Low.
